newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Wiesenthal calls on Swiss to face up to WW2 role.
newsitem.headline: Wiesenthal calls on Swiss to face up to WW2 role.

text.p: Veteran Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal on Thursday urged Switzerland to lay bare the role played by its banks and politicians during the Nazi Holocaust.
But the 88-year-old concentration camp survivor also warned against demonising Switzerland.

"It must be in Switzerland's interest to discover who in the government bore responsibilty.... because it is a part of Swiss history," Vienna-based Wiesenthal said in an interview with Austrian news agency APA.

"But we must treat Switzerland fairly," he continued, recalling the crisis of confidence experienced by Austria a decade ago when former president Kurt Waldheim drew fire for hushing up his wartime past.
"At that time Austrians felt that the whole of the outside world had turned against them," Wiesenthal said.
Waldheim's spell in office from 1986 to 1992 was soured by Washington's decision in 1987 to bar him entry to the U.S.
In recent months Switzerland has similarly been forced to confront its role in World War Two.
Critics have accused the Swiss National Bank of laundering looted Nazi gold. The central bank has denied the charges but acknowledged it did buy gold from Nazi Germany.
Separately, Jewish groups have spearheaded a campaign to force Swiss commercial banks to open records of assets left in their vaults by Holocaust victims.

They have accused the country's biggest bank, Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), of deliberately trying to get rid of crucial evidence after a former watchman saved documents from the shredder. UBS has called the shredding a "regrettable mistake".
Wiesenthal urged Swiss banks to make the money locked in unclaimed accounts available to other victims of Nazism.
"In post-communist countries there are some people who have not received any compensation at all," he said.
"Some suffered a double persecution. When they returned from the concentration camps, the Russians accused them of working for Nazi Germany and banished them to Siberia."
Last week the Swiss banks lifted their traditional secrecy to publish names of lost account holders.

The list of nearly 1,800 dormant accounts appeared in newspapers in more than 20 countries and on the the Internet, the worldwide computer network. The accounts hold some 60 million Swiss francs ($40 million).
Jewish groups say they have pinpointed the names of Nazi perpetrators among those listed. Wiesenthal has proposed these monies be transferred to a central Swiss fund.
"It would be an act of justice if the money...were transferred to the Swiss help fund for Nazi victims," he said.
